docs.title: 01 · Advanced Pronunciation
docs.text: At Level 1 you worked on individual sounds and word stress. At this level the goal shifts to connected speech — the way fluent speakers link, drop, and reshape sounds across word boundaries — plus intonation patterns that carry meaning on their own. These are the features that make the difference between "understandable" and "sounds genuinely fluent."

docs.title: 1. Linking sounds between words
docs.text:
Fluent speech doesn't pause between words the way written text has spaces. Sounds link across word boundaries in predictable ways.

Pattern Example What happens Consonant → vowel turn it off "tur-ni-toff" — the final consonant slides onto the next word's vowel Same consonant meets same consonant big game The two sounds merge into one held sound: "bi-game" Vowel → vowel (with glide) go on A light /w/ glide appears: "go-w-on" /t/ or /d/ + /j/ don't you, did you Merges to "don-cha," "di-ju"

Try reading this sentence at normal speed, linking every word: "Turn it off and get out of the car." Spoken fluently it sounds closer to "Tur-ni-toffn-getou-tovthe-car" — this is completely normal native rhythm, not sloppy speech.

docs.title: 2. Intonation patterns and what they signal
docs.text:
Pattern Shape Used for Falling intonation Pitch drops at the end Statements, commands, wh-questions ("Where do you live?") Rising intonation Pitch rises at the end Yes/no questions ("Do you live here?"), showing uncertainty Fall-rise Drops then rises slightly Politeness, hesitation, implying "but..." ("It's fine... [but]") Rising then falling (listing) Rise on each item, fall on last Lists: "I need bread, ↗ milk, ↗ and eggs. ↘"

A wh-question said with rising intonation ("Where do you LIVE?" ↗) can sound suspicious or aggressive rather than curious — falling intonation is the neutral default for wh-questions, which surprises many learners whose first language treats all questions as rising.

docs.title: 3. Common advanced-level sound issues
docs.text: Issue Example Fix Schwa neglect Saying "to" as /tuː/ instead of /tə/ in unstressed positions Unstressed function words reduce to schwa /ə/ — "I want to go" → /tə/ Over-articulating every word Sounding robotic, over-precise Let function words compress; only content words get full clarity Flat intonation throughout Sounds monotone, hard to follow meaning Vary pitch across the sentence — see section 2 Wrong syllable stress on longer words neCESSary instead of NECessary Check stress on any word over three syllables before using it in speech

docs.title: 4. Worked example — a fluent reading with linking marked
docs.text:
"I've been thinking about it⌣a lot lately, and⌣I think the best⌣option is to just⌣ask⌣him directly. There's no point in guessing what⌣he wants — it'll only⌣end up wasting more time."

Read it once slowly sound by sound, then again treating every ⌣ mark as a seamless join, no pause or glottal stop at the word boundary.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Record yourself reading the sentence in section 1 and the passage in section 4 at normal conversational speed. Then record five of your own sentences, deliberately linking consonant-to-vowel pairs and reducing function words to schwa. Play both recordings back and mark, honestly, where you reverted to pausing between every word — that is your specific practice target for this module.

docs.title: 02 · Idiomatic Expressions & Natural Phrasing
docs.text: Grammatically correct English can still sound stiff or translated if it avoids the idiomatic phrasing native speakers actually reach for. This module builds a working set of high-frequency idioms, phrasal verbs, and collocations for everyday and professional conversation — chosen for how often they actually occur, not for novelty.

docs.title: 1. High-frequency phrasal verbs
docs.text: Phrasal verb Meaning Example get around to finally do something after delay "I finally got around to fixing the sink." put off postpone "Let's not put off the decision any longer." look into investigate "I'll look into the pricing options and get back to you." bring up introduce a topic "She brought up the budget issue in the meeting." run into meet unexpectedly "I ran into an old classmate yesterday." figure out solve/understand "We still need to figure out the logistics." catch up get up to date "Let's catch up over coffee sometime." deal with handle "I'll deal with the customer complaint."

docs.title: 2. Everyday idioms worth knowing (not overusing)
docs.text:
Idiom Meaning Example on the same page in agreement "Let's make sure we're on the same page before the launch." cut corners do something poorly to save time/money "We can't cut corners on safety." a piece of cake very easy "The test was a piece of cake." hit the ground running start productively right away "The new hire hit the ground running." under the weather feeling slightly ill "I'm a bit under the weather today." break the ice ease initial social tension "He told a joke to break the ice."

Caution: one or two natural idioms per few sentences reads as fluent; four in one sentence reads as trying too hard. Native speakers lean on collocations (section 3) far more often than idioms.

docs.title: 3. Collocations — words that habitually go together
docs.text:
Wrong (literal translation) Natural collocation "make a mistake" ✓ vs "do a mistake" ✗ make a mistake, do homework "heavy rain" ✓ vs "strong rain" ✗ heavy rain, strong coffee "take a decision" (some dialects) vs "make a decision" (standard) make a decision "very hungry" vs the stronger natural version starving "very tired" vs the stronger natural version exhausted

Collocations aren't rules you can derive logically — they're memorized in chunks. Whenever you learn a new adjective or verb, learn it paired with the noun or preposition it naturally travels with.

docs.title: 4. Worked dialogue — natural phrasing in context
docs.text:
A: Sorry I'm late — I got caught up in traffic and then I ran into my neighbor on the way out, so I lost track of time.

B: No worries at all. We haven't really gotten started yet — we're still waiting on two more people, so you didn't miss anything.

A: That's a relief. I was worried I'd have to jump straight into the presentation cold.

B: Not at all, take your time. We'll figure out the schedule once everyone's on the same page.

Notice how much of the naturalness comes from phrasal verbs (caught up in, ran into, lost track of, jump into) rather than advanced vocabulary — this is the actual texture of native conversational English.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take five sentences you commonly say in your own life (about work, routines, plans) and rewrite each using at least one phrasal verb or collocation from this module in place of a more literal phrasing. Record yourself saying all five naturally, then check: does each one still sound like something you'd actually say, or does it sound forced? Cut any that feel unnatural and replace with a simpler alternative.

docs.title: 03 · IELTS Speaking Part 2
docs.text: Part 2 is the "long turn": the examiner hands you a task card with a topic and three or four bullet points, gives you 1 minute to prepare notes, and then you must speak for 1-2 minutes without interruption. It's the part that trips up the most candidates, because it's the only section of the whole IELTS test where you have to sustain monologue speech rather than answer short questions.

docs.title: 1. What the task card looks like
docs.text:
Every Part 2 card follows the same format: a topic sentence, then three or four "you should say" bullet points, then a final open-ended question.

Describe a skill you learned that you found useful. You should say: - what the skill is - how you learned it - how long it took you to learn and explain why you found this skill useful.

The bullet points aren't optional extras — they're your built-in structure. Covering all of them (plus the final question) is usually enough to fill the full 2 minutes without running out of things to say.

docs.title: 2. Using the 1-minute preparation time
docs.text:
You get a pencil and paper and exactly 60 seconds. The biggest mistake is trying to write full sentences — there's no time, and you'll end up reading instead of speaking naturally.

Do Don't Write single words or short phrases per bullet Write full sentences Jot a rough timeline/order to speak in Try to script the whole answer word-for-word Note 1-2 specific details (names, numbers, places) Leave bullets blank because you can't think of a "true" answer — invent one Note a linking word for each bullet ("first," "then," "the reason was") Worry about grammar in your notes — nobody sees them

It is completely acceptable to invent or slightly exaggerate your answer. The examiner is scoring your English, not fact-checking your biography.

docs.title: 3. A simple structure that fills 2 minutes
docs.text:
Time Content ~15s Introduce the topic directly ("I'd like to talk about...") ~60-70s Work through each bullet point in order, with one specific detail per point ~20-30s Answer the final question / add a reflection or consequence ~10s A closing sentence, so you don't trail off mid-thought

Running short (under 1 minute) is the single most common Part 2 failure — it strongly signals to the examiner that you struggle to sustain speech, which hurts Fluency and Coherence.

docs.title: 4. Worked example — full 2-minute answer
docs.text:
Card: Describe a skill you learned that you found useful.

I'd like to talk about learning to touch-type, which is something I picked up a couple of years ago. Before that I used to type with two fingers, looking at the keyboard the whole time, which was incredibly slow whenever I had to write reports for work.

I actually learned it using a free typing website that gives you daily lessons — you start with just the home row of keys, and it gradually builds up until you're typing full sentences without looking down at all. I practiced for about fifteen minutes every morning before work, which doesn't sound like much, but it adds up quickly.

It took me around six weeks before I really noticed a difference, and maybe three months before it felt completely natural — to the point where I don't even think about where the keys are anymore.

As for why I found it useful — well, the obvious reason is speed, but what I didn't expect was how much it changed the way I write. Because I'm not distracted by hunting for keys, I can actually focus on what I'm trying to say, so my emails and reports come out clearer and faster. Looking back, it's probably one of the most practical things I've learned as an adult, even though it seemed like a small, unglamorous skill at the time.

This answer covers all three bullets in order, adds specific numbers (fifteen minutes, six weeks, three months), and closes with a reflection rather than trailing off — filling close to the full two minutes naturally.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Part 2 checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I use all 60 seconds to plan, in short phrases only? Full sentences waste time and lead to reading, not speaking Did I address every bullet point on the card? Directly supports Coherence — shows a complete, organized answer Did I speak for close to the full 1-2 minutes? Running under a minute is read as a fluency weakness Did I add at least one specific, concrete detail? Vague answers score lower on Lexical Resource Did I finish with a proper closing sentence? Avoids sounding like you simply ran out of things to say

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick three Part 2 topics (e.g. "Describe a place you'd like to visit," "Describe a person who has influenced you," "Describe a piece of technology you find useful"). For each: time yourself doing exactly 60 seconds of note-taking in short phrases, then record yourself speaking for 1-2 minutes using the structure in section 3. Play each recording back and check it against the section 5 checklist, especially total speaking time.

docs.title: 04 · IELTS Speaking Part 3
docs.text: Part 3 follows immediately after Part 2 and lasts 4-5 minutes. The examiner asks broader, more abstract discussion questions connected to the Part 2 topic — asking for your opinions, comparisons, and predictions rather than personal facts. This is where higher-band candidates separate themselves: Part 3 explicitly rewards the ability to analyze, compare, and speculate in English, not just describe.

docs.title: 1. How Part 3 differs from Parts 1 and 2
docs.text: Feature Part 1 Part 2 Part 3 Question type Personal, factual Single described topic Abstract, opinion-based Answer length 2-4 sentences 1-2 minute monologue Extended answers, examiner follows up Focus You, your life A specific memory/experience Society, trends, general truths Example question "Do you like reading?" "Describe a book you enjoyed." "Do you think fewer people read books nowadays than in the past? Why?"

docs.title: 2. The question types to expect
docs.text: Type Example Comparison (past vs. present) "How has the way people learn skills changed in the last twenty years?" Cause and effect "Why do you think some people struggle to learn new skills as adults?" Speculation about the future "Do you think technology will make certain skills unnecessary in future?" Society-wide opinion "Should schools focus more on practical skills than academic subjects?" Comparing groups "Do you think men and women learn skills differently?"

docs.title: 3. A framework for extended opinion answers
docs.text:
A weak Part 3 answer is a one-line opinion. A strong one takes a clear position and supports it with reasoning and an example — similar in shape to a mini persuasive paragraph.

  1. State your opinion clearly — "I'd say...", "In my view...", "I think it really depends, but generally..."
  2. Give a reason — "mainly because...", "the main factor is..."
  3. Give a concrete example or illustration — "for instance...", "you can see this with..."
  4. Acknowledge the other side (optional but raises band) — "That said, some people would argue...", "Of course, it's not true for everyone..."

docs.title: 4. Worked example — a full Part 3 exchange
docs.text:
Examiner: Do you think fewer people read books nowadays than in the past?

You: I think it really depends on how you define "reading" — people probably read less in the traditional, sit-down-with-a-novel sense, but they're reading constantly on their phones: articles, messages, social media posts. So overall reading volume might not have dropped that much, it's just shifted format.

Examiner: Why do you think some people struggle to learn new skills as adults?

You: I'd say the biggest factor is time — as an adult you've usually got work and family responsibilities eating into your day, so there's just less room for slow, consistent practice, which is really what skill-learning needs. There's also a psychological side to it: adults are often more afraid of looking incompetent than children are, so they avoid practicing in front of others, which actually slows them down.

Examiner: Do you think technology will make certain skills unnecessary in the future?

You: Almost certainly, yes — you can already see it happening with things like handwriting or mental arithmetic, which used to be essential and now matter much less because of computers and calculators. That said, I don't think it's all negative; it usually just shifts what counts as a valuable skill, rather than making people less capable overall.

Each answer takes a position, gives reasoning, and includes a concrete example — the pattern that examiners associate with Band 7+ responses.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Part 3 checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I give a clear position, not just "maybe, I don't know"? Vague non-answers cap your Fluency and Coherence score Did I support my opinion with a reason? Shows Grammatical Range through complex, reasoned sentences Did I include at least one concrete example? Distinguishes strong answers from generic ones Did I use hedging language appropriately ("tends to," "arguably")? Natural for abstract topics — shows nuanced Lexical Resource Did I avoid memorized "template" phrases that don't fit the question? Examiners are trained to spot rehearsed, irrelevant answers

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the five question types from section 2 and write one original question for each, based on a Part 2 topic of your choice. Answer each one aloud using the four-step framework in section 3, aiming for 30-45 seconds per answer. Record yourself and check whether you gave a clear position and a concrete example in every answer.

docs.title: 05 · IELTS Writing Task 1 Basics
docs.text: Writing Task 1 (Academic) asks you to describe visual information — a graph, chart, table, diagram, or map — in at least 150 words, in about 20 minutes. It is not an essay: you are not asked for your opinion, just an accurate, well-organized description of what the data shows. (The General Training version of Task 1 is a letter instead — this module covers the Academic chart/graph version, which is the more common one people mean by "Task 1.")

docs.title: 1. What examiners actually want
docs.text:
They want They don't want An overview sentence identifying the main trend(s) A line-by-line description of every single number Grouped, selective description of key features An attempt to mention every data point Accurate comparison language Your opinion on why the trend happened Correct tense (usually past, sometimes present) Speculation not shown in the data

Task 1 is graded on: Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy — the same four-part structure as Task 2, but "Task Achievement" here specifically means covering the key trends and writing an overview.

docs.title: 2. The four-paragraph structure
docs.text:
Paragraph Content Approx. length 1. Introduction Paraphrase the question in one sentence 1 sentence 2. Overview 1-2 sentences stating the main trend(s), no numbers 2 sentences 3. Body 1 Detail on the first/largest group of data, with figures 3-4 sentences 4. Body 2 Detail on the second group of data, with figures 3-4 sentences

The overview is the single highest-value sentence in the whole response. Many candidates skip it and go straight to describing numbers — this caps Task Achievement regardless of how much detail follows, because the examiner is specifically checking for it.

docs.title: 3. Language for describing trends
docs.text:
Direction Verbs Adjectives/adverbs Increase rose, increased, grew, climbed sharply, steadily, gradually, dramatically Decrease fell, declined, dropped, decreased slightly, significantly, sharply No change remained stable, stayed constant, leveled off — Fluctuation fluctuated, varied considerably, slightly Peak/trough peaked at, reached a low of, bottomed out at —

Comparison language: "X was nearly twice as high as Y," "X and Y were roughly similar, at around 40%," "the gap between X and Y widened over the period."

docs.title: 4. Worked example
docs.text:
Task: The chart below shows the percentage of households with internet access in three countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

The chart illustrates the proportion of households with internet access in Country A, Country B, and Country C over a twenty-year period from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, internet access rose substantially in all three countries over the period, although Country A consistently had the highest level of access throughout, while Country C lagged behind the other two for most of the timeframe.

In 2000, household internet access stood at around 30% in Country A, compared with just 10% in Country B and under 5% in Country C. Access in Country A climbed steadily throughout the two decades, reaching approximately 90% by 2020. Country B followed a broadly similar pattern, though starting from a much lower base, and had caught up to almost 80% by the end of the period.

Country C, by contrast, grew only gradually until around 2010, after which it rose sharply, eventually reaching roughly 65% in 2020 — still the lowest of the three countries, but the gap with Country B had narrowed considerably by the final year shown.

This response has a paraphrased intro, a clear numberless overview, and two body paragraphs with grouped, selective figures rather than a list of every data point.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Task 1 checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I write an overview sentence with no specific numbers? Directly required for Task Achievement Did I group data logically (by category, by time period)? Supports Coherence and Cohesion Did I use a range of trend vocabulary, not just "increased" repeatedly? Raises Lexical Resource Did I stay descriptive and avoid giving reasons/opinions? Task 1 only asks you to report, not explain or judge Is my response at least 150 words? Under-length responses are penalized on Task Achievement

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find a simple line or bar chart online (search "IELTS Task 1 practice chart" for free examples) and write a full four-paragraph response following the structure in section 2, using at least three different trend expressions from section 3. Check your word count is 150+ and that your overview sentence contains no specific figures.

docs.title: 06 · IELTS Writing Task 2 Basics
docs.text: Task 2 asks you to write an essay of at least 250 words in about 40 minutes, responding to a statement or question with your own position, supported by reasons and examples. It carries more weight than Task 1 in the overall Writing band score, so a clear, well-planned structure matters more here than almost anywhere else in the test.

docs.title: 1. The four essay question types
docs.text:
Type Typical wording What's required Opinion (agree/disagree) "To what extent do you agree or disagree?" State and defend one clear position Discussion (both views) "Discuss both views and give your own opinion" Present both sides, then give your own view Problem/solution "What problems does this cause and what solutions can you suggest?" Identify problems, then propose solutions Two-part question "Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development?" Answer both parts explicitly

Identifying the type correctly is the first step — answering a "discuss both views" question as if it were a plain opinion essay is a common cause of a low Task Achievement score, since half the task goes unaddressed.

docs.title: 2. The five-paragraph structure
docs.text:
Paragraph Content 1. Introduction Paraphrase the topic (1 sentence) + a clear thesis stating your position (1 sentence) 2. Body 1 One main idea, explained, with a specific example 3. Body 2 A second main idea (or the opposing view, for "discuss both" questions), explained with an example 4. Body 3 (optional) A third point, or your own opinion if the question is "discuss both views" 5. Conclusion Restate your position in different words + a brief summary of your main reasons

Each body paragraph should follow one idea per paragraph — mixing multiple unrelated points in one paragraph is the most common Coherence and Cohesion penalty at this level.

docs.title: 3. A paragraph-level formula (PEEL)
docs.text: Step Purpose Example Point State the paragraph's main idea "One major advantage of remote work is improved productivity." Explain Say why this is true "This is because employees avoid time-consuming commutes and office distractions." Example Give a concrete illustration "For example, a 2021 Stanford study found remote workers were 13% more productive than office-based staff." Link Connect back to the question "This suggests remote work can benefit both employees and employers."

docs.title: 4. Worked example — opinion essay outline + intro/conclusion
docs.text:
Question: Some people think universities should focus on preparing students for careers, while others think universities should focus on broadening knowledge. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Introduction: There is ongoing debate about whether the primary purpose of universities should be to equip students with job-specific skills or to provide a broad, general education. While both perspectives have merit, I believe universities should aim to combine the two rather than favor one exclusively.

[Body 1 — career-focused view, with example: vocational degrees, employability statistics]

[Body 2 — broad-knowledge view, with example: critical thinking, adaptability in a changing job market]

[Body 3 — your own opinion, with reasoning for a balanced approach]

Conclusion: In conclusion, although career-focused education offers clear short-term employment benefits, a broader education builds skills that remain valuable throughout a person's working life. A balanced curriculum that includes both is therefore likely to serve students best.

The introduction paraphrases the question and states a clear position ("combine the two"); the conclusion restates that position without repeating the same wording.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Task 2 checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I correctly identify the question type (section 1)? Answering the wrong task type caps Task Achievement Does my introduction state a clear position? Examiners look for this specifically Does each body paragraph cover exactly one main idea (PEEL)? Central to Coherence and Cohesion scoring Did I include at least one specific example per body paragraph? Generic, example-free paragraphs score lower Is my essay 250+ words, with a distinct conclusion? Under-length or conclusion-less essays lose Task Achievement marks

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Choose one question type from section 1, write your own practice question in that style, and produce a full five-paragraph essay following the structure in section 2, using PEEL (section 3) for at least two body paragraphs. Check your final word count and confirm your introduction and conclusion state the same position in different words.

docs.title: 07 · IELTS Listening Strategies
docs.text: The IELTS Listening test has 4 sections, 40 questions total, and runs about 30 minutes of audio plus 10 minutes at the end to transfer answers onto the answer sheet (in the paper-based test; the computer version gives 2 minutes instead). Each section is played only once. Sections get progressively harder and shift from everyday, social contexts to academic ones.

docs.title: 1. The four sections at a glance
docs.text: Section Context Speakers Typical difficulty 1 Everyday social conversation (e.g. booking, enquiry) 2 speakers Easiest 2 Everyday monologue (e.g. a talk about a facility) 1 speaker Easy-medium 3 Academic/training discussion (e.g. students and a tutor) Up to 4 speakers Medium-hard 4 Academic lecture/monologue 1 speaker Hardest

docs.title: 2. Common question types
docs.text: Type What it looks like Strategy Form/note/table completion Fill in gaps with words/numbers from the audio Predict word type (name, date, number) before listening Multiple choice Choose one of 3-4 options Options are often paraphrased — listen for meaning, not exact words Matching Match items to a list of options Read all options first; options are usually used only once Plan/map/diagram labeling Label a floor plan or map Track direction words: "next to," "opposite," "turn left" Sentence completion Complete a sentence with words from the audio Check the word limit stated in the instructions ("NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS")

docs.title: 3. Core strategies
docs.text:
1. Use the preview time. Before each section plays, you're given time to read the questions — use every second to predict what kind of answer is needed (a name, a number, a place) and underline keywords.
  2. Listen for paraphrase, not exact matches. The audio rarely uses the same words as the question; if the question says "cost," the speaker might say "the price comes to..." or "you'll need to pay..."
  3. Watch for distractor answers. Speakers often self-correct ("It's on Tuesday — actually, no, sorry, it's been moved to Wednesday") — the final stated information is usually the correct answer.
  4. Never leave a blank. There's no penalty for wrong answers, so always write your best guess even if you're unsure.
  5. Respect word/number limits exactly. Writing three words when the limit is "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS" makes the answer automatically wrong, even if the content is correct.

docs.title: 4. Worked example — a Section 1 style excerpt
docs.text:
Audio (paraphrased example): "So, I'd like to book a room for a conference next month." "Sure — we have a room available on the 14th, but note that's a Saturday, so there's a 20% weekend surcharge. If cost is a concern, the 16th, a Monday, would work out cheaper." "Let's go with the 16th, then, to keep costs down."

Question: What date is the conference room booked for? Correct answer: the 16th Why: the 14th is mentioned first as a distractor, but the speakers settle on the 16th at the end of the exchange — exactly the kind of self-correction pattern in strategy 3 above.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Listening checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I read the questions during the preview time, every section? Predicting the answer type before listening dramatically improves accuracy Did I underline keywords in each question? Helps you track where you are as the audio plays Did I check the word/number limit for each question set? Exceeding it makes a correct answer count as wrong Did I watch for corrections/changes mentioned by speakers? The final version of information is what's tested, not the first Did I answer every question, even with a guess? No penalty for incorrect answers — blanks are pure lost points

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find a free IELTS Listening Section 1 or 2 practice recording online. Before playing it, read the questions and predict, in writing, what type of answer each blank needs (name/number/place/etc.). Play the audio once only, answer without pausing, then check your answers and note which mistakes came from missing a paraphrase versus missing a word-limit rule.

docs.title: 08 · IELTS Reading Strategies
docs.text: The Academic Reading test has 3 passages, 40 questions, and a 60 minute time limit — with no extra transfer time in the computer-based test (in the paper-based version, everything must be written directly on the answer sheet within the same 60 minutes). Passages get progressively longer and more complex, and time pressure — not vocabulary — is the main reason candidates lose marks.

docs.title: 1. The time-pressure problem
docs.text:
60 minutes for 40 questions across roughly 2,750 words of text means you have about 20 minutes per passage, including reading and answering. Reading every word carefully, the way you might in a classroom, is too slow — this module is about targeted reading techniques instead.

Technique What it means When to use it Skimming Fast read for general idea/structure, not detail First pass over a passage, before answering questions Scanning Searching quickly for a specific word, name, date, or number Locating the answer once you know what you're looking for Close reading Careful, full-sentence reading Only for the 1-2 sentences around a located answer

docs.title: 2. Common question types
docs.text: Type Strategy True/False/Not Given (or Yes/No/Not Given) "Not Given" means the information isn't in the text at all — don't confuse it with "False"; a common trap Matching headings Skim each paragraph for its main idea, not detail; headings are often paraphrased, not literal Sentence completion Predict the grammatical type of the missing word before scanning Matching information Scan for named details (numbers, proper nouns) that appear in only one paragraph Multiple choice Eliminate options that contradict the passage or add unsupported claims

docs.title: 3. True/False/Not Given — the trap that costs the most marks
docs.text:
Statement type Meaning True The passage confirms the statement False The passage directly contradicts the statement Not Given The passage simply doesn't mention this information at all — it's neither confirmed nor denied

Example: Passage says "The bridge was completed in 1932 and is still the longest of its kind in the country." Statement: "The bridge was the most expensive one built that decade." → Not Given — cost is never mentioned, so it cannot be marked True or False.

docs.title: 4. A practical reading order
docs.text:
1. Skim the passage first (2-3 minutes) — read the title, first and last sentence of each paragraph, to get the overall structure and what each paragraph covers.
  2. Read the questions, underlining keywords (names, numbers, or distinctive words that are unlikely to be paraphrased).
  3. Scan for each keyword in the passage, using the paragraph map from step 1 to go straight to the likely section.
  4. Close-read only the 1-2 sentences around a located keyword to confirm the actual answer.
  5. Move on if stuck — mark a guess and return only if time remains; one difficult question is not worth losing time for three easier ones later in the passage.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — Reading checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I skim for structure before answering any questions? Saves far more time than reading passage word-by-word upfront Did I distinguish "False" from "Not Given" correctly? The single most common source of lost marks in this test Did I underline keywords in questions before scanning? Makes scanning targeted instead of re-reading the whole passage Did I watch for paraphrased headings/synonyms, not literal word matches? Questions rarely reuse the passage's exact wording Did I move on from a stuck question rather than over-spending time? Protects your ability to answer every question at least once

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find a free IELTS Academic Reading passage online. Time yourself: 2-3 minutes to skim, then 15-17 minutes to answer all its questions using the reading order in section 4. Afterward, check every question you got wrong — note whether the mistake was a False/Not Given confusion, a missed paraphrase, or a timing issue.

docs.title: 09 · Giving a 3-5 Minute Structured Talk
docs.text: Level 1 built a 2-minute short talk. This module extends that to a 3-5 minute structured talk — long enough that a simple opening-middle-end shape isn't enough on its own; you need explicit signposting to keep a listener oriented and enough content depth to sustain several minutes without repeating yourself.

docs.title: 1. Why longer talks need more structure
docs.text: A 2-minute talk can survive on a rough shape held in your head. At 3-5 minutes, a listener loses track of where you are unless you tell them — and you, as the speaker, are more likely to run out of planned content and start repeating points. Both problems are solved the same way: explicit structure.

docs.title: 2. A five-part structure for longer talks
docs.text:
Part Purpose Approx. length 1. Hook/intro Grab attention, state the topic 20-30s 2. Roadmap Tell the listener what points you'll cover, in order 15-20s 3. Point 1 (with example) First main idea, fully developed 45-60s 4. Point 2 (with example) Second main idea, fully developed 45-60s 5. Point 3 + conclusion Third idea + wrap-up, restating the main message 45-60s

The roadmap step is what separates this from a Level 1 short talk — explicitly saying "I want to cover three things: first X, then Y, and finally Z" gives the listener a mental map to follow for the next several minutes.

docs.title: 3. Signposting language
docs.text:
Function Phrases Announcing structure "I want to cover three main points today," "Let's start with..." Moving to the next point "Moving on to...", "The second thing I'd like to mention is...", "That brings me to..." Giving an example "For instance...", "A good example of this is...", "To illustrate..." Returning to the main thread "Going back to what I said earlier...", "As I mentioned..." Concluding "So, to sum up...", "The main takeaway here is...", "In short..."

Signposting phrases cost almost nothing in content but do enormous work for Coherence — they're one of the highest-value additions at this level.

docs.title: 4. Worked example — outline for a 4-minute talk
docs.text:
Topic: Why I think learning a second language is worth the effort

Hook: "I want to talk today about something I get asked a lot: whether it's really worth the time to learn a second language as an adult. My answer is yes, and I want to explain why through three points."

Roadmap: "I'll talk about the practical benefits, then the cognitive benefits, and finally the personal, emotional side of it."

Point 1 (practical): Career opportunities, travel, access to more information — with a specific example (a colleague who got a promotion partly because of a second language).

Point 2 (cognitive): Improved memory and multitasking, delayed cognitive decline — reference a general, well-known finding (without overstating it as fact) and a personal observation.

Point 3 (emotional) + conclusion: Confidence, connecting with people from other cultures — closing with "So while it takes real effort, I think the payoff — practically, mentally, and personally — makes it more than worthwhile."

Notice each point gets a clear signal ("first," "second," "finally") and the conclusion explicitly restates the three points before ending.

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — longer talk checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I state a roadmap near the start? Orients the listener for a multi-minute talk Did I use a signpost phrase before each new point? Makes structure audible, not just present in your head Did each point include a concrete example? Prevents the talk from sounding like a list of abstract claims Did my conclusion restate the main points, not just stop? A proper close is expected at this length Did I hit close to the 3-5 minute target? Under 3 minutes suggests underdeveloped points; well over 5 suggests poor time control

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Choose a topic you know well and outline it using the five-part structure in section 2, writing only short phrases for each part (not full sentences). Record yourself delivering the talk aloud, aiming for 3-5 minutes, using at least four signposting phrases from section 3. Play it back and check it against the section 5 checklist.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Full Mock IELTS Speaking Interview Script
docs.text: This module ties together everything from Level 2: Part 1 short answers, Part 2's 1-minute-prep long turn, and Part 3's extended opinion answers. The project is to run a complete, timed mock Speaking test on your own — the same format examiners actually use, start to finish, in 11-14 minutes total.

docs.title: 1. The full test format, timed
docs.text: Part Duration Content Introduction ~1 minute Examiner confirms identity, asks 1-2 warm-up questions Part 1 4-5 minutes 10-12 personal questions across 2-3 familiar topics Part 2 3-4 minutes 1 minute prep + 1-2 minute long turn + 1 follow-up question Part 3 4-5 minutes 4-6 abstract discussion questions related to the Part 2 topic Total 11-14 minutes

docs.title: 2. Building your own mock script
docs.text:
Since you're self-administering, prepare the questions in advance (so you're reacting live, not reading pre-written answers) — the answers must be spontaneous to be useful practice.

  1. Part 1: Pick 2-3 topics from the Level 1 topic bank (hometown, work/study, hobbies) and write 4-5 questions per topic.
  2. Part 2: Pick one task card in the standard format (topic + 3-4 "you should say" bullets + final question) — see Level 2 Module 3 for the format.
  3. Part 3: Write 5-6 abstract questions that connect logically to the Part 2 topic — see Level 2 Module 4 for the five question types (comparison, cause/effect, speculation, society-wide opinion, comparing groups).

docs.title: 3. Worked example — a full mini mock script
docs.text:
Introduction: "Can you tell me your full name?" / "What shall I call you?"

Part 1 — Topic: Hobbies - What do you like to do in your free time? - How long have you been interested in that? - Do you prefer hobbies you do alone or with other people? - Has your favorite hobby changed since you were younger?

Part 2 card: Describe a hobby you enjoy. You should say: - what the hobby is - how you got into it - how often you do it and explain why you enjoy it. (Follow-up: "Do you think this hobby has taught you anything?")

Part 3 — Topic: Leisure and society - Do you think people have more free time now than in the past? - Why do some people struggle to find time for hobbies? - Do you think hobbies are more important for children or adults? - Will technology change the way people spend their free time in the future?

docs.title: 4. Running the mock and self-scoring
docs.text:
Record the entire session in one continuous take, without pausing to plan — pausing defeats the purpose of practicing under real test conditions. Afterward, self-score using the same four criteria the real test uses:

Criterion What to check in your recording Fluency and Coherence Are there long silent pauses? Do you use signposting/linking words? Lexical Resource Did you use varied vocabulary, or repeat the same words? Grammatical Range and Accuracy Did you attempt complex sentences (not just simple ones)? Were they mostly correct? Pronunciation Is your speech generally clear? Did you use natural stress and intonation?

docs.title: 5. Cheat sheet — mock test checklist
docs.text: Check Why it matters Did I time each part against the real format in section 1? Practicing under real time pressure is the point of a mock test Did I write only questions in advance, not answers? Scripted answers don't train spontaneous speech Did I record the whole thing in one uninterrupted take? Simulates real exam conditions honestly Did I self-score against all four official criteria? Generic "that went well" feedback doesn't drive improvement Did I identify one specific weakness to target next time? Turns the mock test into a concrete practice plan

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Using section 2, build your own full mock script (Part 1 topics, one Part 2 card, Part 3 questions). Record yourself doing the entire 11-14 minute mock test in one take without pausing to plan. Self-score using the table in section 4, and write down one specific, actionable improvement to focus on in your next practice session.

docs.title: Level 3 · Advanced Advanced
docs.text: Goal: reduce fillers and self-correct in real time, push toward IELTS Band 7+ in speaking and writing, and build public-speaking and cross-cultural communication skills for professional and academic settings.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Advanced Fluency Techniques
  2. IELTS Band 7+ Speaking Strategies
  3. IELTS Band 7+ Writing Strategies
  4. Advanced Listening for Academic/Professional Contexts
  5. Advanced Reading for Academic Texts
  6. Public Speaking Basics
